subject: English
topic: Sentence Improvement — Inversion, Idiom Correction and Advanced Grammar (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'Only then he realised his mistake.'

options.option_text: Only then he was realising his mistake.
Only then did he realise his mistake.
Only then he had realised his mistake.
No improvement

questions.explanation: B is correct. After restrictive adverbs like 'only then', 'only after', 'seldom', 'rarely', 'never', 'hardly', 'scarcely' at the beginning of a sentence, SUBJECT-AUXILIARY INVERSION is mandatory. 'Only then DID he realise' (auxiliary 'did' before subject 'he'). This is the same inversion used in questions. Correct: 'Only then did he realise his mistake.' Trap: 'he realised' = no inversion (wrong); 'he was realising' = wrong tense AND no inversion.

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'He runs very fastly in the morning.'

options.option_text: He runs very fast in the morning.
He runs very faster in the morning.
He is running very fastly in the morning.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. FAST is one of the 'flat adverbs' — words that are identical in adjective and adverb form. 'Fast' is BOTH the adjective ('a fast runner') and the adverb ('he runs fast'). 'Fastly' does NOT exist in standard English. Similarly: hard/hard, early/early, late/late, high/high, low/low, far/far. Trap: 'faster' = comparative (no comparison is made here); 'fastly' = non-existent word that sounds logical but is wrong.

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'She is more cleverer than her sister.'

options.option_text: She is more cleverer as her sister.
She is cleverer than her sister.
She is more clever then her sister.
No improvement

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'More cleverer' = DOUBLE COMPARATIVE — both 'more' AND '-er' are used (wrong). The rule: one-syllable adjectives take -er (cleverer); two-syllable adjectives EITHER use -er OR 'more' — never both together. 'Clever' (2 syllables) takes '-er': 'cleverer' ✓. 'More clever' is also acceptable but 'more cleverer' is always wrong. Trap: 'more clever then' = 'then' should be 'than' in comparisons (then=time, than=comparison); 'cleverer as' = wrong conjunction (use 'than' not 'as' in comparisons).

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'I prefer tea over coffee.'

options.option_text: I prefer tea than coffee.
I prefer tea to coffee.
I prefer tea rather than coffee.
No improvement

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Prefer...TO' is the standard formal construction. 'I prefer tea TO coffee.' NOT 'over' (informal American English) or 'than'. SSC uses British/formal grammar → 'prefer X to Y' ✓. For 'would prefer': 'I would prefer to have tea rather than coffee' (infinitive construction uses 'rather than'). Trap: 'prefer tea than coffee' = wrong conjunction (prefer takes 'to', not 'than'); 'prefer...rather than' is valid in the pattern 'would prefer to do X rather than Y' but 'prefer X rather than Y' (without infinitive) is non-standard.

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'Walk carefully lest you should not fall.'

options.option_text: Walk carefully lest you should fall.
Walk carefully lest you might not fall.
Walk carefully so that you should not fall.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. The construction 'LEST...should' ALREADY contains the negative meaning ('lest' = for fear that). Adding 'not' creates a double negative that reverses the meaning. 'Lest you SHOULD fall' = for fear that you might fall (warning). 'Lest you should NOT fall' = for fear that you might NOT fall (absurd — you don't want them to fall, so you warn). Rule: LEST is ALWAYS followed by 'should' (or sometimes bare infinitive), NEVER 'not'. Trap: 'lest you might' = 'might' is wrong (use 'should' with lest); 'so that...should not' = different construction entirely.

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'He is as strong, if not stronger, than his brother.'

options.option_text: He is as strong as, if not stronger than, his brother.
He is as strong, if not stronger as, his brother.
He is stronger if not as strong than his brother.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. The sentence has two comparison structures: 'as strong AS' (requires 'as...as') and 'stronger THAN'. The conjunction must work for both when the middle phrase is removed. 'He is as strong AS his brother' (remove 'if not stronger than'). Both must be complete. 'He is as strong AS, if not stronger THAN, his brother.' Both 'as' (for 'as strong') and 'than' (for 'stronger') are needed. Trap: 'as strong, if not stronger, than' = missing the second 'as' in 'as strong as'; 'stronger as his brother' = wrong (stronger needs 'than', not 'as').

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'The two sisters love one another deeply.'

options.option_text: The two sisters love each other deeply.
The two sisters love themselves deeply.
The two sisters love each one another deeply.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. Grammar rule: 'EACH OTHER' is used when exactly TWO people/things are involved; 'ONE ANOTHER' is used for THREE or more. 'Two sisters' = two people → 'each other' is correct. 'One another' is wrong for a pair. Correct: 'The two sisters love EACH OTHER deeply.' Trap: 'themselves' = reflexive pronoun meaning they love themselves individually (wrong); 'each one another' = non-existent phrasing.

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'Not one of the students have submitted the assignment.'

options.option_text: Not one of the students has submitted the assignment.
None of the students has submitted the assignment.
Not one of the students are submitting the assignment.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Not one' = singular subject → singular verb 'HAS'. 'Not one of the students HAS submitted.' Similar to: 'Not a single person was there.' Trap: 'None of the students has' is also grammatically correct in formal usage (none = not one → singular), but the question asks for improvement of 'Not one...have' specifically → the fix is A ('has'); B would also fix the error but uses 'none' which changes the wording beyond the minimum needed improvement. 'are submitting' = continuous tense (wrong).

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'This is one of the most interesting book I have ever read.'

options.option_text: This is one of the most interesting books I have ever read.
This is one of the more interesting books I have ever read.
This is the most interesting book I have ever read.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'One of the + SUPERLATIVE + PLURAL NOUN' — the noun after a superlative in this construction must be plural. 'One of the most interesting BOOKS' (plural). The original 'book' (singular) is wrong. Trap: 'more interesting' = comparative (only 2 are being compared — not 'one of the most'); 'the most interesting book I have ever read' = grammatically correct but changes the meaning entirely (from 'one of the best' to 'the single best' — that's a different claim).

questions.stem: Select the improved version or 'No improvement': 'He is working very hardly to finish the project on time.'

options.option_text: He is working very hard to finish the project on time.
He is working very hardily to finish the project on time.
He is hardly working to finish the project on time.
No improvement

questions.explanation: A is correct. Like 'fast', HARD is a flat adverb: 'work hard' (not 'hardly' or 'hardily'). Critical distinction: HARD (adverb) = with great effort; HARDLY (adverb) = scarcely/almost not. 'He is working hardly' = he is barely working (completely opposite meaning!). 'Hardily' = non-existent standard word. 'Working very HARD' = working with great effort ✓. Trap: 'He is hardly working' = makes grammatical sense but means the OPPOSITE (he's barely doing any work); 'hardily' = not a real word.
